newsitem.title: USA: Peruvian released after U.S. judge's criticism.
newsitem.headline: Peruvian released after U.S. judge's criticism.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, U.S. Law Correspondent
A Peruvian imprisoned since last May when he sought political asylum here was released after a federal judge harshly criticised immigration officials, his lawyer said on Tuesday.

Julian Calero Salazar, 47, was released from federal prison on Friday after his family posted $100,000 bond, lawyer Michael Deutsch said. Calero Salazar is now living with a sister in Wilton, Connecticut, while his asylum case proceeds. Final arguments are set for March 30.

The Board of Immigration Appeals agreed that Calero Salazar could be released on bail shortly after a hearing last Tuesday in which U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan lambasted government officials for delaying the case for months.
He said he had seen the Immigration and Naturalisation Service act in a "disastrous fashion" on more than one occasion, "But this one takes the cake and I'm not going to stand for it much longer."

Calero Salazar's case had received much attention because Peru had sought his extradition, alleging he was a member of the leftist guerrilla group Shining Path. However, Deutsch argued the charge was contrived and his client fled his native land because of political persecution and fear of Peruvian military police.
Deutsch, legal director for the Centre of Constitutional Rights, said Calero Salazar's wife and father-in-law have been jailed and tortured and his brother-in-law killed.

Indeed, federal prosecutors ended extraditon proceedings in August when Peru failed to supply sufficient evidence against Calero Salazar. An immigration judge granted bail on Sept. 6 after finding that Calero Salazar posed no risk of flight or danger to the community.
But the INS won a temporary stay of the ruling from the Board of Immigration Appeals while it determined if Calero Salazar could be released. He had been kept in solitary confinement.
Calero Salazar had originally been detained when he went to the INS office to seek political asylum on May 30.
A Peruvian farmer who had been living with his sisters in Connecticut, Calero Salazar, was detained because he had entered the United States illegally.
While in detention, he was arrested on June 3 on a separate federal criminal complaint based on a Peruvian arrest warrant.

Federal prosecutors said he had been indicted on "terrorism" charges in Peru and there were five outstanding warrants for his arrest there. They said Peru alleged he was a member of the Shining Path group, which had planned and executed many attacks in Peru, resulting in the deaths of police officers and civilians.
